paras: The assault on Bill Barker was an attack on a Black man by five or six young white men on the river bank opposite Selma, Alabama, on the afternoon of April 8, 1903. The men struck him, took his money and threw him into the river, but he survived; two Alabama dailies reported it the next day, one of them as a joke.
The spot across from the city had lately become a meeting place for crap shooters, and that day several Estelle cotton mill employees had crossed the river for a picnic.

At about 2 o'clock, residents on the Selma side saw one Black man struggling with six young white men across the river. He was struck over the head and thrown into the river while one of the men brandished a razor and threatened to cut his throat. Catching hold of tree limbs in the water, he called for help, and the white men ran away.
By his own account, he had stopped his boat to watch the men shooting craps, showed $3 when asked whether he had money, and was robbed, struck with a stick and thrown in.

Four young men were arrested at the ball park, but the victim said they had not been among his attackers. The Advertiser wrote that the others' names were known to the authorities; no report of further arrests or a trial was found.

The Birmingham Age-Herald headlined its Selma special "Negro Won Money but Got Beating" and likened the attack to a slur-laden song about a Black man and a white man "playing seven-up." The Montgomery Advertiser printed the victim's account of a robbery but called a different story, from people who said they were not eyewitnesses, the "most credited" one. No Black-press coverage was found.

The victim appears as "Bill Barker" in the Age-Herald and "Will Baker" in the Advertiser. In the Advertiser's "most credited" version, he joined the game, won all the men's money and was beaten and robbed when he refused to return it, though only the robbery account came from a participant.

reader.title: Assault on Bill Barker at Selma
bases: A group of five or six young white men, not officials, beat a Black man, took his money and threw him into the river while threatening him with a razor; he survived (A1, A2).

Two separately written Selma dispatches in different papers agree that a Black man was struck, thrown into the river and threatened with a razor by about six young white men on the afternoon of April 8 (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Onlookers across the river (Age-Herald special)
accounts.gist: Residents on the Selma side saw one Black man and six young white men struggle; he was struck over the head and thrown in the river while one of the men brandished a big razor, and the men ran when he called for help.

accounts.label: Victim's account
accounts.gist: Coming up the river in his boat, he stopped to watch six white men shooting craps; asked if he had money, he showed $3, and the men robbed him, struck him with a stick, threw him into the river and threatened to cut his throat with a razor.

accounts.label: 'Most credited' version (people in the vicinity who were not eyewitnesses)
accounts.gist: He asked to join the game, won all the men's money, and was beaten and robbed when he refused to give it back; fearing trouble, the men threw him in the river and might have killed him had they not been frightened away.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald treated the attack as comedy, headlining 'NEGRO WON MONEY BUT GOT BEATING' and likening it to the song 'Nigger and white man playing seven-up,' though its narrative described the white men's attack plainly.
The Montgomery Advertiser printed the victim's account of robbery but called the craps-winnings story, from people who were not eyewitnesses, 'most credited'.

conflicts.note: Both are Selma dispatches of the same day; neither is clearly better evidence.

versions.value: Robbery: the men asked if he had money, took his $3, struck him and threw him in the river (victim's account)
He won the men's money at craps and was beaten and robbed when he refused to return it ('most credited', from non-eyewitnesses)
A dice win, implied by the 'seven-up' framing and headline

conflicts.note: The victim's account is the only one attributed to a participant; the 'most credited' version came from people who said they were not eyewitnesses.

info: About 2 o'clock in the afternoon of April 8, 1903
A clump of bushes on the river bank opposite Selma (the south bank), a spot described as a rendezvous for crap shooters
One Black man, named 'Bill Barker' by the Age-Herald and 'Will Baker' by the Advertiser, described as a 'strapping six-footer'; he survived
No crime was charged against the victim; in the 'most credited' version he had won the white men's money at craps and refused to give it back
Young white men playing craps; the Advertiser notes that several Estelle cotton mill employees had gone across the river that day for a picnic
The victim caught on tree limbs and called for help; the attackers ran off. No report of further arrests, a hearing or a trial was found.

sources.note: Selma special of April 8: six young white men beat a Black man, threw him in the river, one brandishing a razor; names him Bill Barker; mocking 'seven-up' headline; text cut off mid-sentence.
quotes: NEGRO WON MONEY BUT GOT BEATING
saw the negro struck over the head and then saw him picked up and thrown into the river, while one of the young men seemed to be attempting to get at him, brandishing a big razor.
The negro called lustily for help and the white men scampered away.

quotes: He pulled $3 out of his pocket and he claims the young white men set upon him and after taking his money away from him struck him with a stick and threw him into the river.
The story that is most credited is that the negro came along and asked to be allowed to get in the game.
Four young men were arrested at the ball park, but the negro who suffered violence says they were not in the crowd.
